A São Paulo businessman has been arrested by police on suspicion of sending a game console stuffed with explosives to the electronics store of a rival in an attempt to kill him. The device then exploded. On Monday, Military Police executed a warrant against Everton Yoshizumi Lima, who is suspected of perpetrating the outrageous attack, G1 reports.

On October 23, 2026, at around 5:30 pm, a delivery person dropped off a video game console at an electronics repair shop, with the cover that it was being left for modifications requested by the customer. Police say the device had an explosive planted inside that was programmed to detonate upon receipt. "Unaware of its contents, the store owner put the video game console in a drawer and continued working," the report states. The device ignited and exploded, causing severe damage and injuring two people: the owner of the store and a friend who was at the scene. The whole thing was captured on video, which you can see by expanding the tweet below:

Empresário é preso suspeito de enviar videogame com explosivos que detonaram em loja de eletrônicos de Santo André, Grande SP https://t.co/EqXSlkM1J9 #g1 https://t.co/H3naAgNzlVNovember 16, 2026

The device was found to have two explosive charges of the same magnitude inside, but only one of the devices went off, possibly limiting the capacity for damage and injury. The report notes that investigators believe the intent of the device was to kill the victim, given the amount of explosives. The console was delivered to the store by an unsuspecting motorcyclist who was working for a delivery app company and had no idea they were carrying a bomb.

The request appears to have been traced back to Lima, who is the main suspect in the attack. Lima purportedly owns other electronics stores in the area, including two on the same street where this store was recently opened, labeling the motive as "business competition." "The new store had been advertised through a social media campaign and the distribution of flyers," the report states. "Annoyed by the competition, the suspect allegedly decided to eliminate the competitor, according to the line of investigation."

According to the report, Lima was arrested during the course of an investigation into a possible motorcycle theft. It appears that Lima was the owner of the target vehicle, and that police visited in advance, suspecting someone might try to steal it. While checking his data, it was found that Lima had an outstanding arrest warrant for his suspected involvement in the attack.

#10142. DeepSeek-V4: a million-token context that agents can actually use

DeepSeek released V4 today. Two MoE checkpoints are on the Hub: DeepSeek-V4-Pro at 1.6T total parameters with 49B active, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 284B total with 13B active. Both have a 1M-token context window. The benchmark numbers are competitive, but not SOTA. It doesn't matter. The real innovation is how DeepSeek v4 is designed for efficient large context length support, and hence as one of the best candidates for agentic tasks.

Focusing on long running agentic workloads. Running a frontier open model as an agent today breaks in predictable ways. The model stops. You reprompt. The trace blows past the context budget, or the KV cache fills the GPU, or tool-call round trips degrade halfway through a long task. V4 is built to fix these known failures, and point the way for the community to follow.

This post covers three things: what the architecture does differently to make long-context inference cheap, the agent-specific post-training decisions that compound on top of it, and some takeaways from the paper that help reason about these changes.

A 1M context window is just capacity, not performance. Whether you can use it depends on the cost of every forward pass at that depth. For an agent running a long tool-use trajectory (a SWE-bench task, a multi-step browse session, a terminal session with hundreds of commands), every tool result is appended to the context, and every subsequent token pays the full attention cost against everything that came before.

Two numbers matter: single-token inference FLOPs and KV cache size. Both grow with sequence length. At 1M tokens, DeepSeek-V4-Pro requires 27% of single-token inference FLOPs compared with DeepSeek-V3.2, so it runs faster on the same hardware. It also uses 10% of the KV cache memory. V4-Flash drops these numbers even further: 10% of the FLOPs and 7% of the KV cache.

If we compare the KV cache memory against a established architecture like grouped query attention with 8 heads, stored in the usual bfloat16 format, DeepSeek v4 requires roughly 2% the cache size. This makes it much easier to deploy for very large context handling.

Figure 1: benchmark comparison (left), per-token FLOPs and accumulated KV cache against sequence length (right).

The efficiency gain comes from splitting attention into two mechanisms and interleaving them across layers.

Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) compresses KV entries by 4x along the sequence dimension using softmax-gated pooling with a learned positional bias. A lightning indexer (FP4, ReLU-scored multi-head dot product) picks the top-k compressed blocks per query. It inherits the sparse-selection idea from DeepSeek Sparse Attention in V3.2, but runs it over blocks that are already 4x shorter than the original sequence. The indexer's search space shrinks with it.

Figure 3: CSA. The compressor collapses every 4 tokens into one compressed KV entry. The lightning indexer picks the top-k compressed blocks per query. A sliding-window branch handles the most recent uncompressed tokens.

Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) compresses KV entries by 128x and drops the sparse selection. Every query attends densely to every compressed block. The compressed sequence is short enough that dense attention is cheap.

Figure 4: HCA. A heavier compressor (128x vs. 4x) followed by dense attention over the compressed stream, with the same sliding-window branch for recency.

The layers alternate between CSA and HCA. Different layers carry different attention patterns, and forcing one mechanism across all of them wastes capacity. In V4-Pro's 61-layer stack, layers 0–1 are HCA, layers 2–60 alternate CSA and HCA, and the MTP block at the end runs sliding-window only.

Both paths use FP8 storage for most KV entries and BF16 only for the RoPE dimensions. The lightning indexer inside CSA runs in FP4. These storage choices compound with the compression ratios to produce the 2% KV cache figure.

Figure 2: overall architecture. Attention layers alternate between CSA and HCA. Feed-forward layers use DeepSeekMoE. Residual connections are replaced with manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC).

Efficient long-context attention is necessary for agent workflows but not sufficient. The paper describes three post-training and infrastructure choices that target agent use cases directly.

V3.2 kept reasoning traces across tool-result rounds but discarded them whenever a new user message arrived. For an agent handling a single user turn, this was fine. For multi-turn agentic workflows, where the user sends a follow-up after the agent has already chained several tool calls, the model lost its accumulated reasoning and had to reconstruct state.

V4 preserves reasoning content across user message boundaries when the conversation contains tool calls. The model retains the complete reasoning history across all rounds, including across user turns. This allows a coherent, cumulative chain of thought over long-horizon agent tasks. For conversational use without tools, the old behavior is preserved: reasoning is flushed on each turn to keep context concise.

Figure 7: thinking with tools (top) preserves reasoning across all turns. Thinking without tools (bottom) discards reasoning at each new user message.

V4 introduces a |DSML| special token and an XML-based tool-call format. The XML format reduces escaping failures compared to JSON-in-string tool calls, a common failure mode when models emit nested quoted content.

The schema separates string parameters (passed as-is with string="true") from structured parameters (passed as JSON with string="false"). This removes a class of parsing errors around numbers and booleans that JSON tool-call formats routinely hit.

The agent behavior was trained with RL against real tool environments. The paper describes the sandbox infrastructure built for that purpose. DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec) is a Rust platform that exposes four execution substrates behind one Python SDK: function calls, containers, microVMs (Firecracker), and full VMs (QEMU). A single cluster runs hundreds of thousands of concurrent sandboxes.

Three DSec features matter for agent training: fast image loading via layered 3FS storage (so RL rollouts do not wait on container startup), preemption-safe trajectory replay (so interrupted training steps resume without re-running tool calls), and a uniform API across substrates (so training harnesses target function calls or full VMs without rewriting). These infrastructure decisions underpin the agent benchmark scores.

The knowledge and reasoning numbers are competitive but not leading. The agent numbers are where V4-Pro-Max separates from the field.

Specific numbers from the agent section of Table 6:

In the paper's internal R&D coding benchmark, 30 curated tasks across PyTorch, CUDA, Rust, and C++, V4-Pro-Max hits 67% pass rate, versus 47% for Sonnet 4.5 and 70% for Opus 4.5. In a survey of 85 DeepSeek developers using V4-Pro as their daily driver, 52% said it was ready to replace their current primary coding model and 39% leaned toward yes.

The long-context retrieval numbers are in Figure 9. MRCR 8-needle accuracy stays above 0.82 through 256K tokens and holds at 0.59 at 1M.

Figure 9: MRCR 8-needle retrieval. V4-Pro-Max stays above 0.82 through 256K and holds at 0.59 at 1M.

Four checkpoints are on the Hub. The instruct models use FP4 for MoE expert weights and FP8 for everything else. The base models are FP8 throughout.

Both instruct models support three reasoning modes: Non-think (fast, no chain of thought), Think High (explicit reasoning in blocks), and Think Max (maximum reasoning effort with a dedicated system prompt). Think Max requires a context window of at least 384K tokens. The recommended sampling parameters across all modes are temperature=1.0, top_p=1.0.

The V4-Pro numbers on SWE Verified, MCPAtlas, and the internal R&D benchmark put it at parity with frontier closed models on agent tasks. The open question is how the community's tool harnesses adapt to the |DSML| schema and whether the interleaved thinking gains transfer to out-of-domain agent frameworks.

Figures in this blog post are from the technical report at DeepSeek_V4.pdf.

According to my personal tests DeepSeek V4 Flash (Non-thinking mode) passed the Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval test on both 32k and 435k actual prompt tokens with a 100% result across depths of 0-100%. In no-needle negative control with the NOT_FOUND instruction, the model also returned 100% correct failures, reducing the risk of contamination and false positives.

So thinking mode may degrade behaviour in some tests.

Phison’s Pascari X201P meets its rated specs and pairs 12 GB/s sequential writes with a steady 600K random write IOPS, making short work of AI checkpoints. It gives ground at low and moderate queue depths, where QD1 writes and mixed workloads lag, and it ran warm on our bench.

Mixed-workload performance trails at middle QDs

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Phison is serious about enterprise storage, and the Pascari X201P was not released lightly; it came in the night, under NDA, alongside this week’s Supercomputing 2026 event. The drive is part of the Performance X-Series, which handles intensive workloads where consistency is the name of the game. We were nevertheless pleasantly surprised by its write performance, with a steady 12 GB/s for sequential and over 600,000 random write IOPS, considering it’s marketed at the 1 drive write per day (DWPD) endurance point.

Part of that surprise comes from the fact that this is Phison’s read-intensive PCIe 5.0 data center drive, a successor to the X200P. It comes in the U.2 form factor — which can be more convenient in many cases — from 1.92TB to 30.72TB, and an E3.S version from 3.84TB, in both single- and dual-port models. It stands next to its mixed-use sibling, the X201E, which is the one rated for 3 DWPD. What makes the X201P exciting, in part, is its own 16-channel X2 controller and the flash that’s inside.

This drive is aimed at AI, analytics, and database servers, with its case made in the 4K 70/30 mix at higher queue depths. It passed Phison’s one-million-IOPS mark at QD128 in our testing of the 15.36TB model, and the drive met all of its rated specs, though its random read rating required polled I/O to reach on our bench. It faced challenges with QD1 writes, log commits, and the middle range of our mixed sweeps. Given its blend of performance, capacity, and endurance, we consider it a very competent entry from the company that was perhaps better known in the consumer SSD market until recently.

The drive met or beat every rated performance figure that we can test, which should be the target of any enterprise SSD released today. If there’s an exception, it’s due to how we test; Phison lists a ceiling of 3,250K IOPS for 4K random read, which is higher than our bench allows with our interrupt-driven I/O, which we use rather than a polled approach. We also run a polled test on every drive for cases like this, and our result was 3,283K IOPS at the same queue depth Phison specifies, which shows the drive does exceed its specification.

Datacenter NVMe SSD v2.0, with v2.6 telemetry features

PCIe 5.0 x4, single port (2x2 dual-port models offered)

ISE, SED (TCG Opal 2.02) or non-SED; AES-XTS 256-bit

512-byte and 4,096-byte, each with optional metadata

Six: 25 W, 22 W, 20 W, 18 W, 15 W and 12 W maximum

Host-controlled thermal management supported

Our sample is in the U.2 form factor, 15mm thick. We have the single-port SKU, ISE model XP208H0815T3P3216T310, with firmware X2WM6026. Some data we previously saw from the drive was reportedly on X2WM6025, but we confirmed X2WM6026 for all relevant results. We mounted the drive on a PCIe 5.0 x4 add-in card adapter for U.2, standing upright in the slot.

Phison did not provide firm hardware details, but we were able to discover some things on our own. The flash was probably the easiest, as the company claimed it was a 321-layer part. That can only be SK hynix’s V9 TLC, which is not flash we’ve tested before in any product. It’s exceptionally fast and uses a three-deck design, which is relatively new for TLC flash. The flash could be credited with some of the exceptional performance measurements we see on the drive.

As for the proprietary controller, we’ve heard that it’s using a combination of the standard Arm Cortex-R5 — these would be the main cores — with AndesCore RISC-V on the side. We’ve seen the latter before on the Phison E28 consumer SSD controller, which did have some enterprise-like aspects to it. The E28 is the newer design, built on a 6nm process with Andes’ newer N45 cores alongside the N25F, while the X2 is a 12nm part that, as far as we can tell, sticks with N25F-class co-processors.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

In this case, the X2 has twice the flash channels, which enables a superior level of performance out of TLC flash, as in enterprise you do not rely on pSLC. That mix of cores sets the X2 apart from other 16-channel PCIe 5.0 enterprise controllers: Marvell’s Bravera SC5 and Silicon Motion’s SM8366 rely on Arm cores throughout, whereas Phison pairs its Cortex-R5 cores with small RISC-V co-processors.

#10139. How to build scalable web apps with OpenAI's Privacy Filter

All three are built on gradio.Server, which lets you pair custom HTML/JS frontends with Gradio's queueing, ZeroGPU allocation, and gradio_client SDK. In all these apps, gradio.Server plays the same backend role, and that consistency is exactly what makes it really powerful.

Try it at ysharma/OPF-Document-PII-Explorer.

User problem. You want to read a PII-heavy document (a contract, a resume, an exported chat log) with every detected span highlighted by category, a filter in the sidebar, and a summary dashboard up top. The reading experience should feel like a normal document, not a form.

What gr.Server does here. You could wire this up in Blocks with gr.HighlightedText and a sidebar, and it would work. The reading experience we wanted (serif body, category filters that toggle CSS classes client-side instead of re-running the model, a summary dashboard that doesn't force a page re-render) was easier to hand-author than to compose. gr.Server lets us serve the reader view as a single HTML file and expose the model behind one queued endpoint:

Note the decorator: @server.api(name="analyze_document"), not a plain @server.post. That's the piece that plugs the handler into Gradio's queue, so concurrent uploads are serialized, @spaces.GPU composes correctly on ZeroGPU, and the same endpoint is reachable from both the browser and gradio_client with no duplicated code. The browser calls it with the Gradio JS client:

User problem. You want to share an image or any screenshot (a Slack thread, a receipt, a Stripe dashboard) with black bars over the PII. You want to toggle bars on and off, drag them to reposition, or draw one by hand for anything the model missed, then export the result.

What gr.Server does here. gr.ImageEditor supports layered annotation and is a reasonable starting point for image redaction. The workflow we wanted (per-bar category metadata, toggle all bars in a category at once, client-side PNG export at natural resolution with no server round-trip) was cleaner to build on a custom frontend. gr.Server hands back pixel rectangles from one queued endpoint and lets the canvas own everything else:

The frontend invokes it with client.predict("/anonymize_screenshot", { image: handle_file(file) }), the same pattern as above. Toggles, drags, new-bar drawing, and PNG export all happen in the browser; edits never round-trip to the server.

User problem. You want a pastebin that redacts before sharing. You paste a log line, an email, a support ticket. You get two URLs back. The public one serves the redacted version with , , placeholders, following the redaction convention from the official blog examples. The private one is gated by a token you keep and shows the original with spans highlighted.

What gr.Server does here. This app needs two distinct GET routes for the same paste ID, one public and one token-gated, and the URL shape matters because the reveal URL is the thing you keep. gr.Server works here because it's a FastAPI app underneath — which is also why @server.api and plain @server.get can sit side by side in the same process. Note: this can also be built with gr.Blocks() by mounting custom routes with FastAPI :

A daemon thread evicts expired pastes every 30 seconds. The whole service, including storage, is about 200 lines of application code because everything lives in one process.

The split across all three apps is the same — anything that touches the model goes through @server.api, everything else stays on plain FastAPI routes:

@server.api gives you Gradio's queue (serialized requests, correct @spaces.GPU composition on ZeroGPU, progress events) and it's what the browser hits through @gradio/client. The same endpoint is also what gradio_client users hit from Python — one function, two SDKs, no duplicated code. Plain @server.get/@server.post are reserved for the static surfaces: HTML pages, file lookups, cheap dict reads. That's the rule of thumb from the gradio.Server intro post, and it's what makes these three apps feel consistent even though their UIs are very different.

One gap I keep hitting for clinical notes outside EN: taxonomy coverage ≠ “run the same 8 labels on another language/domain.” Locale clinical text needs entity classes and distractors that the EN consumer schema doesn’t encode; otherwise you measure a different product than the one you deploy. Synthetic labeled notes help for that coverage test before anyone claims compliance.

Curious whether you’ve tried feeding clinical-style notes (even synthetic) through the same 8 labels and where the misses concentrate.

#10138. How to Build a Unified Lead Tracking Pipeline for Web Forms and Phone Calls

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A visitor clicks a search ad, submits a quote request, and calls your sales team ten minutes later. The form integration creates a CRM contact. The phone platform records a call. By Friday, the marketing report shows two leads, while sales remembers one conversation that turned into a deal.

Both systems captured something useful. The problem is that neither record explains how the two interactions belong together.

A unified tracking pipeline gives forms and calls a common event format, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to CRM outcomes. It also needs to survive a less tidy reality: repeated callbacks, missing campaign data, delayed updates, and a CRM that occasionally refuses requests.

This tutorial builds the core of that pipeline with JavaScript and PostgreSQL. We will capture campaign parameters, define a shared event contract, and persist events alongside the work needed to deliver them. Provider authentication and CRM requests belong in adapters around this core, using the documentation for the services you choose.

Before writing an endpoint, decide what you are counting. A phone call can produce several status callbacks. A person can submit two forms. An existing customer can contact sales about a new purchase.

Use separate identifiers for these different things:

This separation prevents two common mistakes. Deduplicating by call ID alone can discard later status updates. Counting every callback as a lead inflates demand.

For this implementation, each event is unique within a tenant and source. A tenant is the business whose data you are processing; the source identifies a website or provider account. The same provider event ID can therefore appear in two accounts without causing a collision.

Keep the original interactions even after you connect them to one contact. The form and the call are both useful evidence. Your reporting layer decides whether they represent one opportunity.

Campaign parameters are easiest to capture when the visitor first arrives. Waiting until the form submission can lose them if the visitor has already moved to another page.

Google's campaign URL documentation explains the roles of utm_source, utm_medium, and utm_campaign. The following helper reads those fields and a few optional ones, without copying the entire query string:

const params = new URL(url).searchParams;

"utm_source", "utm_medium", "utm_campaign",

return Object.fromEntries(keys.flatMap(key => {

The browser's URLSearchParams interface handles query parsing and decoding. It saves you from writing string-splitting code that breaks on encoded characters.

Run this helper through your site's existing consent and attribution flow. Where storage is permitted, associate the result with an opaque attribution reference in your backend and retain that reference through the visit. A later form submission sends the reference; the server resolves it within the correct tenant and visitor session. The form must still work when attribution storage is unavailable.

Keep first-touch and current-touch records separately if you need both. Overwriting the first campaign every time someone returns makes the eventual report answer a different question.

Treat campaign labels as untrusted input. Visitors can edit query strings and hidden fields. Validate them on the server, escape them when displayed, and never use them as authorization or as the sole evidence for commission payments. Avoid putting names, email addresses, or other personal information in UTM values.

Missing tags also need careful handling. An empty UTM object only tells you that no accepted UTM values were captured. Classifying a visit as direct, organic, or referral requires additional evidence and an explicit attribution rule.

Forms carry browser context naturally. Phone calls need a bridge between the number dialed and the marketing interaction that prompted the call.

There are two useful levels of precision. A number assigned to one campaign can identify that campaign. Dynamic number insertion can support a more detailed association by displaying tracking numbers according to a visitor or session mapping. That association depends on the provider's number allocation and expiry rules.

Providers differ in how they implement this, and in what they expose beyond it, such as keyword-level reporting or conversation analysis. If you are still choosing one, this comparison of attribution software with call tracking is a useful starting point. At the integration boundary, check which event identifiers, attribution fields, delivery mechanisms, and authentication options your configured product exposes.

Keep that provider-specific work in an adapter. Its job is to turn an authenticated notification into your event contract and resolve any attribution reference supported by the provider's data. The application schema below is an internal contract; each provider adapter translates its documented payload into that contract.

Store the basis of a match with the attribution record. For example, session_match, campaign_number, and unknown make different levels of evidence visible to reporting. If a number has been reassigned, use the mapping valid when the call occurred, not whichever mapping happens to be current when the callback arrives. If the evidence is ambiguous, leave the association unresolved.

Caller ID is a separate issue. A shared office number, a withheld number, or an outdated contact record can make automatic identity matching unreliable. A confirmed CRM contact ID or an authenticated account provides a stronger link. Treat a matching phone number as a candidate for reconciliation rather than proof that two records belong to the same person.

A shared event envelope lets the rest of your application work with a small, predictable vocabulary. Here is an illustrative call event:

"occurred_at": "2026-11-06T10:14:00.000Z",

The event ID identifies this occurrence. The interaction ID groups it with other events for the same call. contact_ref can remain empty until you have enough evidence to connect the interaction to a contact.

Keep contact details in a controlled contact store and campaign details in an attribution store. The references above point to those records; they are not credentials and must not grant access on their own.

The following factory checks the shared envelope. Each adapter still needs its own validation for provider fields and the contents of data.

"form.submitted", "call.started", "call.completed",

export function makeEvent(input, trusted) {

const ids = [trusted.tenantId, trusted.source,

if (ids.some(id => typeof id !== "string" ||

throw new TypeError("Invalid event identifiers");

throw new TypeError("Unsupported event type");

const time = Date.parse(input.occurredAt);

if (typeof input.occurredAt !== "string" ||

new Date(time).toISOString() !== input.occurredAt) {

throw new TypeError("Expected a canonical UTC timestamp");

attribution_ref: input.attributionRef ?? null,

Resolve trusted from server configuration and the authenticated integration. Never let a submitted tenant_id choose whose records a webhook can write. Resolve contact and attribution references within that same tenant.

For a form, issue a submission ID and reuse it when retrying the same submission. Generate a new one when the visitor deliberately starts another inquiry. Preserve the originally accepted timestamp as well. For a phone event, prefer the provider's stable event ID. If the provider documents a sequence number, a call ID plus that sequence can identify an occurrence within a provider account.

Twilio's call resource documentation provides a concrete example: call progress callbacks include a SequenceNumber, and separate HTTP requests can arrive out of order. Preserve that sequence in the adapter. A late “ringing” event should remain in the history without replacing a newer terminal state.

Authenticate before calling this factory. Use the provider's supported validator and the exact request representation it requires. Twilio's webhook security guide describes signature validation, including the importance of the request URL and payload. Other providers may use different mechanisms. Public form endpoints need their own input limits, abuse controls, and appropriate CSRF protection.

Consider a failure between these two operations: the application saves an event, then crashes before scheduling its CRM update. The event exists, but nothing is waiting to deliver it.

A transactional outbox addresses that gap. Save the event and a delivery task in the same database transaction, then let a worker process the task. AWS explains this dual-write problem in its transactional outbox guidance.

Here is a compact schema. received_at records ingestion time, while the envelope retains the event's original occurred_at value.

received_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, source, event_id)

id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,

available_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, source, event_id)

REFERENCES lead_events (tenant_id, source, event_id)

The ingestion function below accepts a pg pool and a normalized event. Install pg in your Node.js project, save the function as persist.mjs, and initialize the pool using your application's database configuration.

export async function persistEvent(pool, event) {

const key = [event.tenant_id, event.source, event.event_id];

const values = [...key, JSON.stringify(event)];

await client.query("BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED");

ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, source, event_id) DO NOTHING

WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND source = $2 AND event_id = $3

const error = new Error("Event ID reused with new data");

INSERT INTO crm_outbox (tenant_id, source, event_id)

return { inserted: inserted.rowCount === 1 };

PostgreSQL's INSERT documentation defines the conflict handling used here. The unique key makes duplicate detection hold across application processes. A duplicate with the same normalized payload creates no second task; reuse of the key with different data raises a conflict for investigation.

This depends on immutable event bodies. Do not add a fresh receipt timestamp, random identifier, or current CRM status to the normalized payload on each delivery. Store later enrichment separately or emit a new event. Otherwise an ordinary retry will appear to be a conflicting event.

The function deliberately uses one database client throughout the transaction, as required by the node-postgres transaction documentation. Parameter values are passed separately from SQL, following its parameterized query guidance.

After this function commits, acknowledge the notification using the response expected by the sender. An identical duplicate should also receive a successful acknowledgement. If persistence fails, return the appropriate failure response and rely on the configured retry or reconciliation process. A success response sent before durable storage can turn a temporary database failure into a missing event.

For voice integrations, distinguish an informational status callback from a request asking your application how to handle a live call. They can require different response bodies, as explained in the Twilio webhooks FAQ.

The outbox gives you durable work to process. It does not make a remote CRM operation happen exactly once.

Imagine the CRM saves an update, but the worker crashes before setting processed_at. When the task runs again, the same request may reach the CRM twice. Design for that case explicitly.

Use a stable external identifier for each contact, opportunity, and activity, and check which deduplication guarantees the destination supports. HubSpot's contacts API documentation, for example, describes upserts using unique properties. Support for a contact upsert does not automatically make every associated activity or workflow idempotent. Verify the behavior of each operation you send.

If the destination cannot deduplicate a create request and a timeout leaves its result uncertain, reconcile that operation before repeating it. A local “sent” flag alone cannot prove whether the remote write happened.

The worker should claim due tasks, commit a recoverable lease, and perform network calls outside the database transaction. A lease allows another worker to recover work after a crash. When multiple workers poll the outbox, PostgreSQL's SKIP LOCKED behavior can help claim separate rows, but the lease and its recovery logic still need to be implemented.

Retry transient failures with increasing delays and jitter. Respect the destination's rate-limit instructions. Send persistent validation failures to a review queue with a useful error category, and provide a way to replay them after correction. The schema above is the ingestion foundation; a production worker needs lease fields, failure details, and a retry policy appropriate to its destination.

Also preserve ordering where it changes meaning. If two events update the same contact or opportunity, process them serially or reject stale updates using a stored version. A historical event should not move a won opportunity back to an earlier stage.

Once both channels reach the CRM, connect them to the result the business cares about. A form submission is an inquiry. A completed phone call is a technical outcome. Neither alone establishes that a lead qualified or a purchase happened. If agents record call dispositions, such as whether a call was qualified or transferred to a closer, that field is a richer signal than call completion status alone.

Have the CRM or the system that owns the transaction emit explicit outcome events, such as lead.qualified and deal.won. Include the internal opportunity ID and the original outcome time. Model reversals or cancellations explicitly if they affect revenue reporting.

Then choose the unit behind each metric. For a report about opportunities acquired during a particular month, a qualification rate can use qualified opportunities divided by all opportunities in that acquisition cohort. Counting qualification events received during the month would answer a different question and could include older inquiries.

Deduplicate opportunities before calculating channel totals. A person who submits a form and calls about the same purchase should retain both interactions, while the opportunity receives credit according to your chosen attribution rule. Label that rule in the report so first-touch and last-touch numbers are not compared as though they measure the same thing.

Measure data quality alongside performance. Track unresolved attribution, duplicate deliveries, ingestion failures, and the age of the oldest pending outbox task. Once several sources and destinations feed the same reports, a data observability platform can watch these signals across the whole pipeline instead of relying on checks inside a single worker. An apparently quiet campaign may actually have a broken integration.

Operational logs should contain enough context to investigate failures without becoming another customer database. Use internal references and error categories, and avoid dumping webhook bodies into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet provides guidance on excluding or protecting sensitive values.

A successful form submission proves little about retries or missing data. Before connecting production traffic, test the cases that could distort reporting or lose an inquiry.

Run database cases against PostgreSQL with separate connections so the tests exercise actual constraints and transaction behavior. Use the provider's test tools or signed fixtures for webhook authentication. Test CRM retries against a sandbox with the destination's real duplicate-handling rules.

Start rollout with one form and one phone source. Trace a known inquiry from its captured campaign through its interactions to its CRM outcome. Reconcile event totals against the source systems over the same time window, allowing for delivery delays. Expand once that path is explainable and failures are visible.

The same adapter pattern extends to inquiries that start offline, such as leads collected at a trade show and exported as a CSV or XLSX file. Import each row as a form.submitted event with the event as its source, a stable row identifier as event_id, and the original capture time as occurred_at. Because the outbox treats an identical event as a duplicate, re-importing the same export won’t create a second CRM task.

What is a unified lead tracking pipeline?

It is a workflow that converts inquiries from different channels into a shared data model, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to business outcomes. Forms and calls keep their own interaction records, while contacts and opportunities provide the relationships needed for reporting.

Can I connect a phone call to a website visit?

Sometimes. Dynamic number insertion can provide a session or visitor association when the provider's mapping is available and valid. A campaign-specific number usually supports campaign-level attribution. If the caller uses a saved number, switches devices, or calls after a mapping expires, the available evidence may be less precise.

Handle duplicate delivery and identity resolution separately. Stable event IDs and a database constraint prevent repeated notifications from producing repeated work. Connecting several interactions to one contact or opportunity requires a separate matching policy, with ambiguous cases left unresolved until there is enough evidence.

Should a completed call count as a conversion?

Only if that is the conversion your report explicitly measures. A completed call does not establish that a prospect qualified or bought something. Keep technical call status separate from CRM outcomes and use the latter when reporting qualified demand or revenue.

Do I need a message broker for this architecture?

You can begin with PostgreSQL and an outbox worker if that setup meets your throughput and latency needs. A broker becomes useful when several consumers need independent delivery, or when buffering and scale justify the additional operations. In either case, retries still require idempotent consumers.

What happens when tracking consent is unavailable?

Keep the inquiry flow usable and apply your site's existing consent rules to optional attribution collection and storage. Accept permitted form or call data, leave unavailable attribution empty, and avoid reconstructing a visitor identity through fingerprinting. Reports should expose that missing context instead of inventing a campaign match.

#10137. Jensen’s exit could be Google’s TPU moment

Good morning. Today I’m rewatching Tenet to better picture Robert Pattinson in his new role, sighing over the inevitability of delivery drones triggering PTSD symptoms, and laugh-cringing at some of these Bit.ly link hijack stories from the weekend. Plus, prayers to anyone who had to find a last-minute hotel room during last week’s flying nightmare.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

In the immediate fallout of Jensen Huang’s humiliating resignation from Nvidia, coverage will focus on how the company plans to continue without its beloved former CEO, the world’s biggest champion of open-source AI and the proliferation of GPUs across borders. But in the long term, there’s an argument to be made that Google will be one of the largest winners of the shake-up, with a market opening up to competition outside of Nvidia’s CUDA moat.

While Colette Kress, the interim CEO, is unlikely to make any drastic changes to the company’s roadmap, the reality is that Nvidia’s competitors in the semiconductor space have desperately been working to unseat the market leader, and without Jensen at the helm, customers may be more likely to pursue alternatives.

For years, Google has offered its TPUs, or Tensor Processing Units, as a solution for AI training and inference, but they’ve been largely locked to its Google Cloud infrastructure. That’s changing now that the company is opening up sales to third parties and has announced it will bring TPU capacity to Oracle’s cloud beginning in 2027.

Google’s latest generation of TPUs is specialized; here’s how the company describes the lineup in its recent announcement post:

While flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning (inference), TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack.

Google isn’t comparing its new TPUs directly to Nvidia’s offerings, and clock-for-clock, even the most powerful TPU 8i Max doesn’t touch Vera Rubin for sheer performance. But this generation should be much more competitive for a few reasons: it’s more power efficient in certain configurations, and Google made it easier to translate coding workflows optimized for CUDA to work with its TPUs.

Back in October, Google open-sourced TorchTPU, which it co-developed with Meta’s PyTorch team, to let developers use familiar PyTorch workflows on TPUs with minimal code changes. That won’t make every custom CUDA operation portable or eliminate performance tuning, but reducing the effort required to try an alternative may change the buying decision. Customers don’t need to abandon Nvidia outright for Google to increase its TPU market share, or for Nvidia to face more pressure on price.

Alongside Broadcom and MediaTek, Google is taking on the Nvidia behemoth, and in the short term, it will almost certainly see a large upside in sentiment. But in the longer term, with scaling pressure lowering margins for Nvidia, Google’s specialized and more efficient TPUs may be a primary beneficiary of this sea change. They could also offset a slowdown in Search as Google’s shift to Cloud continues apace.

If you’re a sucker for Android nostalgia like I am, a new website lets you relive the glory days of Android 2 through 7 without resorting to finding an old Nexus phone on eBay. Android Time Machine is an extremely vibe-coded experience, but once you get past the bad vibes, the ability to play around with some of the earliest versions of Android in your phone’s browser becomes magical pretty quickly.

Over the past few days, the one-two punch of Microsoft’s 365/Exchange outage and the FAA’s ground stop shows just how vulnerable everyone is to the effects of seemingly brittle tech infrastructure.

The FAA describes a flood of connection attempts that destabilized its telecommunications network, affecting aircraft communications and radar feeds. Investigators identified sites in Arkansas and Texas that were undergoing router and wire replacements, but even days after the stop was lifted, there’s still no clear underlying cause.

Meanwhile, the Microsoft 365 outage lasted about 30 hours, with service restored to the remaining customers and regions late Friday. Microsoft says that a “latent defect” introduced into its network code in a July update wasn’t triggered until a few days ago, when high loads led to cascading failures across the company’s servers worldwide.

While neither AI nor cyberattacks were to blame, individually and together the two outages add urgency to getting companies to shore up their defenses and redundancies in a world where we’re overly reliant on digital systems.

Finally, if you’re into DIY projects, you’ve likely heard of TRMNL, the company that makes very cool and slightly overpriced ePaper displays that can be programmed to do basically whatever you want with them.

Now, the company has just revealed a 31.5-inch color ePaper version, encased in a custom wood frame, that sells for nearly $2,000. It can be mounted on a wall without internet, using a microSD card and a 20,000mAh battery, for months of gorgeous art displays, or kept powered and connected to the internet to be used as a (very large) home dashboard.

I want one very badly, but I’ve already chosen my $2,000 poison.

The Justice and Commerce Departments have announced an investigation into the company previously run by the woman officials have accused of being a Chinese spy while having an affair with Jensen Huang while he was Nvidia's CEO.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A criminal investigation into Megaspeed has been confirmed by the United States Justice and Commerce Departments, with a joint statement saying that they will “bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.” Authorities believe that Megaspeed is one of a raft of companies that may have circumvented export rules designed to limit the sale of advanced AI chips, like those built by Nvidia, to approved companies and countries. The company is at the heart of the recent Jensen Huang scandal, which saw him resign from the company last week.

Megaspeed was added to Nvidia's no-sell list in June 2025, the statement reveals, but a New York Times report claims that a Malaysian Megaspeed subsidiary continued to receive large shipments of Nvidia chips for a full eight months after that date. It's believed that Nvidia's export-controlled Blackwell and H200 chips were shipped to Speedmatrix, either via third parties or directly from Nvidia itself, before being handed off to China. Nvidia has argued that it was given Commerce Department permission to ship the components to Megaspeed. Notably, Nvidia continues to list Megaspeed as a cloud partner.

The new criminal investigation follows a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed that first kicked off in 2024 over possible export violations. By May 2025, it had requested Nvidia's data relating to sales it made to Megaspeed, and by June, officials visited Megaspeed and even interviewed Alice Huang, the now-former executive who is allegedly a Chinese spy. Ms. Huang is also the woman that then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with before resigning his position earlier this month. Following that visit, the Justice Department took the lead in the investigation into Megaspeed.

Joint Statement from Department of Commerce and Department of Justice on Megaspeed Investigation. https://t.co/aAdtN9aDfFNovember 17, 2026

Megaspeed has long been accused of being a front for an AI component smuggling operation. In October 2025, an investigation claimed that it had helped move around $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips into China by importing them and then re-exporting them to the country. Megaspeed says that it complies with all laws and that the woman at the center of the affair scandal, Ms. Huang, is no longer at the company. The Chinese government has also dismissed claims that she was a state spy.

The joint Commerce and Justice Departments' statement pointed to its strong track record when prosecuting chip smugglers to date. 17 defendants across a total of six investigations have been charged so far, with more likely to follow. A Californian man was recently arrested after being accused of smuggling more than $300 million worth of export-restricted Nvidia chips to China. He now faces up to 20 years in prison.

#10135. Introducing NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni: Long-Context Multimodal Intelligence for Documents, Audio and Video Agents

Benchmark highlightsBuilding on Nemotron Nano V2 VL, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni delivers substantial visual gains and adds entirely new audio and video+audio capabilities - while also leading another open-weights omni model, Qwen3-Omni, in many domains.

Efficiency highlightsCompared to other open omni models with the same interactivity, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni delivers 7.4x higher system efficiency for multi-document use cases and 9.2x higher system efficiency for video use cases Figure 1. Total system throughput for multi-document and video use cases sustained by each model at a fixed per‑user interactivity threshold (tokens/sec/user)

At a high level, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is aimed at five classes of workloads:

This is not only about OCR. The model is positioned for long, messy, high-value documents where understanding depends on layout, tables, figures, formulas, section structure, and cross-page references. Think contracts, technical papers, reports, manuals, multi-page forms, or compliance packets. The model can handle 100+ page documents.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni includes strong speech understanding capabilities that enable high-quality transcription across diverse audio conditions. It handles long-form audio with varying speakers, accents, and background noise. These capabilities can be integrated into broader workflows, allowing spoken content to be transcribed, analyzed, and combined with other modalities for tasks like summarization, question answering, and cross-modal reasoning.

Many enterprise and developer workflows depend on mixed audio and visual evidence: screen recordings with narration, training videos, meetings with slides, tutorials, product demos, customer support captures, and long-form video archives. Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is built to reason over those inputs jointly.

The Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model is specifically trained for agentic computer use, enabling it to assist with tasks in graphical user interface (GUI) environments. Its capabilities include interpreting screenshots, monitoring the state of the user interface, grounding its reasoning in on-screen visuals, and helping with action selection or workflow automation.

The model is designed for more than perception. It excels at reasoning-intensive tasks that require synthesizing information across long context windows, multiple modalities, and structured or semi-structured evidence. It can carry out multi-step reasoning, perform calculations, and connect signals from text, images, tables, and other inputs to arrive at coherent, well-supported answers.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni uses a unified encoder-projector-decoder design. The language backbone is Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B, paired with the C-RADIOv4-H vision encoder and the Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v2 audio encoder. The modality-specific encoders connect into the LLM backbone through lightweight projectors.

Figure 2. Model architecture of NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni 30B-A3B

The model backbone interleaves three key components: 23 Mamba selective state-space layers for efficient long-context processing; 23 MoE layers with 128 experts, top-6 routing, and a shared expert for conditional capacity; and 6 grouped-query attention layers to preserve strong global interaction and expressivity.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni combines state-space models, attention, and MoE in a unified design that maintains strong reasoning performance while remaining practical for long, multimodal contexts.

On the vision side, the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni replaces the tiling strategy used in the v2 model with dynamic resolution processing at native aspect ratio. Each image can be represented using a variable number of 16 x 16 patches, with a minimum of 1,024 to a maximum of 13,312 visual patches per image. For square images, this is equivalent to 512 x 512 and 1840 x 1840, respectively.

That flexibility is critical for handling high-resolution, complex visual inputs such as OCR-heavy documents, financial tables, slides, research figures, screenshots, and GUI layouts—especially when both fine details and overall structure need to be understood together.

For video, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni uses a dedicated Conv3D tubelet embedding path. Instead of embedding each frame independently, every pair of consecutive frames is fused into a single "tubelet" before the ViT, halving the number of vision tokens the language model has to attend to. This allows us to either double the number of frames with the same token budget, or halve the number of tokens with the same number of frames

EVS is an important feature, enabled during inference time, that drops redundant video tokens after the vision encoder. This reduces latency and improves throughput while maintaining accuracy. The first frame of the video is kept entirely, then for each subsequent frame, EVS keeps the “dynamic” tokens where the video is changing and drops the “static” ones where nothing has changed from the previous frame. We combine this with Conv3D to enable superior compression: Conv3D fuses tokens from pairs of frames into one, and then EVS prunes redundant static information.

The audio side is powered by Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v2, connected to the backbone through its own 2-layer MLP projector. Audio is sampled at 16 kHz, and the model is trained with inputs up to 1,200 seconds (20 minutes), while the LLM max context length supports 5+ hours.

This represents a shift from traditional VLM pipelines by enabling native audio processing within a shared multimodal sequence, allowing audio, visual, and text tokens to be jointly modeled. This is crucial for scenarios like narrated screen recordings, video Q&A where speech alters visual meaning, long-form instructional or meeting content, and tasks requiring temporally grounded multimodal reasoning.

Each encoder is connected to the LLM with a lightweight 2-layer MLP projector that maps encoder features into the shared embedding space. Once projected, vision, audio, and text tokens are interleaved and processed jointly.

This design keeps the overall system modular while still enabling genuine cross-modal reasoning inside the backbone itself.

The SFT stages are trained on NVIDIA H100, scaling from 32 to 128 nodes depending on the stage. The stack uses Megatron-LM, Transformer Engine, and Megatron Energon, with tensor parallelism, expert parallelism, sequence parallelism, context parallelism for the long context stages, online sequence packing, and selective activation recomputation.

Post-SFT reinforcement learning uses NeMo-RL and NeMo Gym with a Megatron backend. The RL infrastructure used a Ray-based distributed setup across B200 and H100 clusters, plus multimodal deduplication, so repeated rollouts do not multiply image, video, and audio memory.

We open-source substantial parts of our training code.

We introduce multi-environment text and omni training in Nemotron 3 Nano Omni. Our text RL training stage happens across diverse environments in Nemo-Gym, which evaluates the model’s ability to perform sequences of actions such as tool calling, writing code, and multi-part planning that satisfy the verifiable criteria.

Omni RL trains the model to reason across images, video, audio, and text within a unified framework, covering tasks from single-modality to fully multimodal scenarios. A diverse verifier suite evaluates outputs across formats like multiple-choice, math, GUI grounding, and ASR, while intentionally including unanswerable cases to teach the model to abstain when evidence is insufficient rather than hallucinate.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is trained on an enhanced dataset that emphasizes high-quality reasoning across multiple modalities. We significantly expand task coverage and introduce synthetic data for complex reasoning scenarios where public datasets are limited. To support this, we build task-specific, multi-stage pipelines for scalable synthetic data generation.

As one example, we generated approximately 11.4M synthetic QA pairs (~45B tokens) from a large corpus of real-world PDFs using NeMo Data Designer. This dataset is used to strengthen long-context document reasoning during post-training and delivers a 2.19× improvement in overall accuracy on MMLongBench-Doc.

We detail the full pipeline evolution, including failure analysis and key lessons learned, in our Data Designer developer note. The note also includes nine runnable pipeline recipes that can serve as starting points for building your own document-understanding datasets.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni can analyze and reason over long documents such as financial reports, academic papers, product manuals, etc. The following example retrieves financial metrics across a 100+ page document to calculate another metric:

Figure 3: Stylized example from the MMLongBench-Doc benchmark

The model was prompted to answer the question as follows:

The model is capable of long-context retrieval, structured extraction, table/chart reading and multi-page reasoning all in one go.

Nemotron-3 Nano Omni performs joint audio-visual analysis, both locally for specific scenes and globally across the entire video. This enables it to answer complex questions that require cross-modal reasoning—such as identifying specific visuals shown exactly when a certain topic is mentioned in the audio.

Nemotron 3 Omni can be integrated into agentic computer-use systems to reason over user intents, analyze GUI elements, and execute actions to accomplish tasks.

Nemotron-3 Nano Omni can analyze charts, figures shown in images, along with audio files to generate any commonalities, discrepancies across the media.

Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni can interpret and reason about general audio, including soundscapes and environmental sounds.

A long-context, multimodal document understanding benchmark

I'm running parakeet-tdt 0.6b-v3 + 1.1b and faster-whisper-v3-turbo as part of a 7-pipeline local stt benchmark on my dropbox corpus (pdf's, images, ppts, keynotes, wavs, mp4s, ...) from meetings and other personal projects on a 4090, so seeing the parakeet encoder + mamba-moe + c-radiov4 combo here is the architectural step i was hoping someone would make.

#10134. Google’s new ‘Fast Switch’ feature leaks, lets you use one number on two Android phones

Similar to a recent iPhone feature, Google appears to be working on “Fast Switch” as a way to share one SIM and phone number on two Android phones at once, and it sounds pretty cool.

Through the SIM Manager app on Android, the folks over at Android Authority noticed strings that tell a pretty clear story.

A new feature called “Android Fast Switch” would let you “use your phone number on up to two phones,” with the SIM automatically switching to “whichever phone you unlock.”

“Android Fast Switch” sounds nearly identical to Handoff on iPhone, a feature that lets iPhone owners share one SIM between two iPhones and quickly switch devices on the fly.

Other strings explicitly say that you can “Use a SIM on two phones” and specify that both devices would need to be logged into the same Google account. One phone would be the “Primary” with the other as a “companion.”

There are still plenty of unknown details here, including what data might sync between devices as well as how carriers will respond. On iPhone, carriers either charge extra for this feature ($5 at T-Mobile, $10 at Verizon), or don’t support it at all (AT&T). We also don’t know what devices may be supported – this could easily end up as a Pixel-only affair.

As per usual with these early teardowns, though, the actual launch of a feature like this could be weeks, months, or even years away. Still, the idea itself is rather exciting.

iPhone’s Handoff feature always sounded useful, but I personally always questioned why it would be useful on iPhone. With so little variety in hardware, the utility of switching between two iPhones seems somewhat dubious, outside of perhaps using a Mini or Air as a situational device alongside a Pro device.

On Android, the combinations are endless. It all just depends on what devices Google supports. What devices would you switch between?

The noose is tightening for Chinese AI labs that need U.S. AI GPUs to train their models.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

CNBC reports that Nvidia has started warning its customers that impending legislation to clamp down on countries accessing AI GPUs remotely via data center rentals could put them in trouble with U.S. authorities. Chinese tech companies could take advantage of the performance of American AI hardware through a loophole in U.S. regulations. Instead of importing Nvidia chips, which are under export controls, they instead look to data centers located abroad and export their data instead. This is what Chinese AI lab Moonshot is apparently trying in Europe, which is why the U.S. Department of Commerce, through the Bureau of Industry and Security [PDF], released an interim final rule closing this loophole.

According to the report, Nvidia has been messaging chip buyers to warn that RASA could expose both Nvidia and chip buyers to legal risk.

The U.S. House of Representatives has already passed a bill called the Remote Access Security Act (RASA) that addressed this specific loophole, but it’s been in limbo in the Senate for over ten months now. It remains unclear if the Jensen Huang affair and suspected espionage scandal will help speed up its approval, but scheduling could be tight with only about 31 calendar days remaining before the Senate's adjournment. But even before any of these regulations are approved and published, the company is already taking steps to protect its customers and has started requiring partners that 51% of their services should go to non-Chinese clients. It has also required its partners to join Nvidia’s Fleet Intelligence tracking system if they want to retain their official partner status

It’s unclear if these changes have been planned over time or were a reaction to the renewed scrutiny that Nvidia is facing. But even though Jensen Huang is now out of the company, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that it’s unclear if the former Nvidia CEO was aware of the alleged smuggling operations and instead laid the blame on the entire company. Nvidia itself has taken steps to improve its security and export control teams by establishing an oversight committee that will be in charge of its “national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management,” and would work with third-party experts in law, national security, and trade compliance.

These measures would further tighten the noose around China’s AI GPUs. Even though it has several domestic chip makers, many AI operators still prefer Nvidia chips for their performance and reliability. There have even been allegations that Alibaba and ByteDance, some of China’s biggest tech companies, prefer training their LLMs in Southeast Asia to bypass bans and restrictions. So, if the U.S. finally shuts down this loophole, we can expect these companies to scramble and find a replacement for the Nvidia GPUs they could access right now.

#10132. Samsung’s Galaxy S27 redesign is ‘100%’ confirmed, leaker says – do you like it? [Poll]

Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series is getting a redesign, with a reliable leaker saying it’s definitely happening. But, do you like it?

To say that Galaxy smartphone design has been stale is a bit of an understatement. The same core design has been in use for over half a decade at this point, with only the smallest tweaks in the past few generations. And it’s been a problem, too. While Samsung insists that the vertical triple camera array is the company’s “core identity,” it also means that the industry’s move to magnetic wireless charging and accessories are essentially incompatible with Galaxy devices.

We’ve seen repeated leaks of the Galaxy S27 series so far with a new full-width camera island on the Ultra and Pro models, and leaker Ice Universe says that this design is now “100%” confirmed, with the final design having two larger camera lenses on the left side, a smaller lens on the bottom right, and a flash above that. We saw this same design in a leak earlier this month, which Ice said at the time was “wrong,” presumably because the flash was replaced by a fourth camera in the dummy unit.

But the question at this point is, do you even like this new look?

Personally, I’m on the fence. I’m thrilled Samsung is finally doing away with the table-rocking, Qi2-ruining vertical array, but I’m not exactly happy we’re getting an iPhone clone as a result. I’d say beggars can’t be choosers, but this is Samsung we’re talking about – I think it’s fair to ask for a bit more.

#10130. AMD attacks Nvidia's FP64 emulation at SC26, touts native double-precision on Instinct MI430X — says Ozaki schemes fit less than 10% of HPC workloads and triple memory use and emulated FP64 is a poor fit for many HPC workloads

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

AMD says Ozaki FP64 emulation is no replacement for the real thing when it's needed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) opens in Chicago this week, AMD is indirectly needling Nvidia about the lack of native FP64 data type support in its data center GPU products. FP64, or double-precision floating-point math, is widely used in the high-performance scientific computing and simulation fields that are the focus of SC26. For those customers, AMD is trumpeting the value of its latest Instinct MI430X accelerator for customers that still need native FP64, like national laboratories and supercomputing centers.

Over the past few years, Nvidia has reallocated die area on its data center GPUs to favor the lower-precision matrix math that boosts the operations needed for much of modern AI inference. That reallocation only makes business sense, as the total addressable market for AI compute has exploded while the demand for double-precision math in large supercomputing installations has remained flat by comparison.

To make up for the lack of native FP64 support, Nvidia has turned to techniques that allow it to emulate FP64 operations using methods like the Ozaki schemes. But AMD claims this kind of emulation is nowhere close to a replacement for native double-precision processing for a few reasons—hence continued development of specialized products like the MI430X.

For one, AMD notes that Ozaki emulation assumes that the workload in question resembles a dense general matrix multiply (GEMM). In its own application profiling, the company says "less than 10%" of HPC workloads perform dense GEMM operations, so this emulation is a good replacement for native compute. Dense linear algebra is the one common workload for which AMD says Ozaki emulation is a natural fit.

For workloads like sparse iterative linear algebra, stencils and hydrodynamics, high-order finite element analysis, Monte Carlo and particle transport, and classical molecular dynamics, AMD says developers still need strong FP64 vector performance for the best results.

Furthermore, even for workloads that map well onto GEMM operations, AMD says matrix sizes must be large in order to achieve the best performance, and that might also not be a given for every operation. The operands of those matrices also have to be sized well to the hardware, as incorrectly scaled operands can reduce performance. The FP64 vector math capabilities of the MI430X are insensitive to those operand sizing issues.

Beyond those stumbling blocks, AMD also notes that using Ozaki emulation methods can cause the memory footprint of an application to balloon, requiring up to three times more capacity than native FP64 would.

Since HBM capacity is directly tied to GPUs in modern supercomputing installations, fitting a workload to a machine that can only emulate FP64 operations could have cascading effects on the number of GPUs and compute nodes required, causing knock-on challenges for the floor area, power, and cooling required to support the system.

AMD says the high 432GB of HBM4 memory capacity per MI430X node allows its customers to provision fewer GPUs and compute nodes in a system, saving on networking, power, and floor space.

In addition to its FP64 HPC performance, AMD positions an MI430X-powered supercomputer as an AI inference platform for developing workloads that utilize those models as part of the research process. But there are some key differences between those systems and the Helios rack-scale accelerator powered by MI455X GPUs from the same CDNA 5 architectural family.

Each MI430X GPU offers 9.2 PFLOPS of theoretical FP4 compute performance for inference, but that should be understood in the context of the whopping 40.3 PFLOPS of FP4 compute from each AI-focused MI455X accelerator.

Beyond raw performance, the native scale-up domain size of four MI430Xs over AMD’s Infinity Fabric interconnect when coupled with a sixth-generation EPYC host CPU pales in comparison to the domain size of 72 MI455X accelerators in a Helios rack. AMD says this interconnect is optimized more for latency-sensitive operations rather than a massive scale-up domain.

Of course, every customer and user of such a system will have different requirements, and institutional supercomputing installations usually aren’t trying to do double duty as cloud inference providers.

For scientists and engineers whose AI models of choice work well within the 1.72 TB of aggregate HBM4 capacity and 93.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth offered by four MI430X's working together across the 12.3 Tbps of scale-up bandwidth available within such a node, the inference performance of each node is likely more than up to the task of the kinds of AI applications that need to be run alongside double-precision compute workloads.

In any event, the MI430X can already count several supercomputing design wins in its corner. The upcoming Discovery supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the Alice Recoque installation in France, the LUMI-AI system at Finland’s CSC, and the Herder system in Germany will all take advantage of the native FP64 support offered by the MI430X.

AMD’s continued support for native FP64, even as Nvidia retreats from that capability in its products, will doubtless be a point of pride for its architects and engineers, even as those institutional supercomputers will be dwarfed by both AMD and Nvidia-powered AI inference installations the world over. The company's semi-custom silicon design chops and chiplet experience give it the flexibility needed to tailor products like the MI430X to these specialized markets instead of pursuing a one-size-fits-all approach.

As the Senior Analyst, Graphics at Tom's Hardware, Jeff Kampman covers everything that has to do with graphics cards, gaming performance, and more. From integrated graphics processors to discrete graphics cards to the hyperscale installations powering our AI future, if it's got a GPU in it, Jeff is on it.

#10129. UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The UK is betting on domestic AI and cyber investment to reduce reliance on US tech — but security leaders question whether the funding is too fragmented and too late.

The UK has announced major investments in strengthening its cyber defenses, designed to stave off the rise of faster, more complex attacks enhanced by AI tools. In late October, the government unveiled a funding package of approximately $800 million to strengthen cyber defenses and AI security investments.

The move comes as Kanishka Narayan, the UK's minister of artificial intelligence, said in a speech last month that "it seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber-defenses will be breached." He cited the recent trend of misaligned models escaping containment, citing the OpenAI incident in June during which an agent hacked an Australian government health agency.

But the UK government is also pushing toward another, related goal: digital sovereignty. In his speech, Narayan emphasized the need to "build in Britain to keep the public safe in Britain" and become less dependent on foreign providers, which has become a common goal for some countries following the US government's export control order for Anthropic earlier this year.

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

"We want the world's leading companies investing here, but we will not accept dependence as the price of that investment," Narayan said.

But industry-watchers argue that government investment to strengthen cyber-defenses while also achieving greater sovereignty by encouraging homegrown tech might be difficult to do all at once.

Two turning points appear to have shifted government policy in the UK and Europe this year, both involving the same US company: Anthropic. The first came with the AI company's unveiling of Project Glasswing in April for its Mythos frontier model, which sparked concerns about a coming "vulnpocalypse" for enterprise security teams.

"It created an almighty whirlpool of conversations," says Tim Williams, CEO of London-based Quod Orbis, which specializes in continuous controls monitoring. "And then there were lots of concerns about what that meant, and everybody seemed to panic. I think that panic has settled down now."

But another event — the Trump administration's ban on foreign nationals using Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models has had a far more lasting effect. The ban didn't just impact overseas companies and government agencies; the export controls effectively forced Anthropic to pull all access to the two models for several weeks.

The implications of abruptly losing access to valuable — and perhaps critical — AI technology through a sudden change in US policy accelerated an already growing conversation about reducing dependency on American tech companies. A crucial part of the UK government's funding package is designed to fuel British AI startups and invest in home-grown companies.

Related:AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進

It's a solid idea, but infosec professionals see two issues with that approach. First, the funding package is split up between a number of initiatives, with approximately £154 million of the £600 million total devoted to strengthening current cyber-defenses, for example.

"If you look at the amount that they're putting into it, is that enough? Is that significant?" Williams asks.

Secondly, the UK is already well behind the curve with fueling homegrown AI and cloud companies. Amir Khan, managing director at Wire, tells Dark Reading that there's been chronic under-investment in emerging technologies in the country, which has led to missed opportunities in the past.

"In the UK, we had DeepMind before it was sold to Google [in 2014]," Khan says. "Had they known the impact that DeepMind would have now, would they still have sold it, or doubled down on it? Who knows? But it's another example of a large organization that grew in the UK, leaving to go to the US."

In fact, due to that kind of ongoing tech emigration, Khan says you could argue that the last good thing to come out of the UK's technology industry was Cambridge Analytica — a company that became embroiled in a scandal involving Facebook.

Related:UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

Time and again, experts have argued that organizations can't counter AI-driven threats effectively without AI-enabled defenses. But that complicates matters for the UK, which is looking to achieve tech sovereignty in the aftermath of the Anthropic ban.

For one, in some part because of the issues outlined above, many of the major AI companies — OpenAI, Meta, SpaceXAI (now SpaceX Super Intelligence), and Palantir Technologies — are also based in the US. And while there are plenty of AI startups these days, those companies may not have the scale needed for national defense systems.

Additionally, there's also the cost component. Williams says many of Quod Orbis' customers are looking to reduce their dependency on a single vendor or provider, whether it's for cloud, software, AI, or other technologies. "There's no question that, in speaking to our clients, that concentrated risk is a concern for them," he says.

But moving from, for example, one cloud provider to four or five can be challenging, especially for mid-market organizations, he says. They may not have the budgets of large enterprises, and they probably rely more heavily on the commercial discounts that the cloud giants like AWS, Microsoft, and Google Cloud Platform provide. "If they're spreading that investment out across multiple cloud providers, that can become more expensive for them," Williams says.

Khan agrees and points to the recent example of France migrating off Windows for government workstations and moving to Linux. But leaving the Microsoft ecosystem will require France to add several more technologies from different vendors. "That, for me, defeats the purpose because you've essentially taken away one provider and pulled in six," he says. "That doesn't really give you the flexibility you want."

Khan argues the UK sometimes sets the wrong target for tech sovereignty. "We talk as though we have to build every chip, every cloud, and every application ourselves," he says. "As you can imagine, that's an enormous undertaking, and it doesn't really get to the heart of the issue. For me, the questions are, can we make our own decisions about the technology that we depend on? Can we operate it on our terms?"

The UK can retain such operational authority, he says, by choosing providers and vendors that build that kind of customer controls directly into their products and services; for example, Khan notes that Wire offers customers a private cloud option for the messaging platform that organizations can control and operate based within whatever country they're located.

Whichever providers or vendors the UK government chooses, officials should be asking several key questions before investing: who holds the encryption keys, who can interrupt the service, and how realistic is it to move off that technology?

In the meantime, the UK government will continue to focus on strengthening the country's cyber defenses through these investments and efforts like the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill currently. But Williams is unsure if they will be enough.

"It's a step in the right direction, absolutely," he says. "But is it the investment I would expect to see in terms of being really concerned about the threat to the UK?"

Rob Wright is a longtime reporter with more than 25 years of experience as a technology journalist. He has a keen interest in malvertising activity and the certificate authority industry, and has written extensively on both topics.
